Star Fox developer Velan: How to survive as a North American game studio
Guha and Karthik Bala on how they won over Nintendo, keeping costs low and working with IP
Christopher Dring
11 hours ago
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Velan Studios’ Guha and Karthik Balak on…
Its Nintendo partnership
Surviving the modern game industry
US dev costs
The IP opportunity
When I saw that Nintendo’s new Star Fox remake was developed by Velan Studios, I got excited. Finally, I had an excuse to invite Guha and Karthik Bala onto The Game Business Show.
If you’ve never encountered the Balas, they’re 35-year game making veterans who founded Vicarious Visions and worked on some huge franchises, including Guitar Hero, Tony Hawks, Spider-Man and Skylanders.
I’ve met them numerous times since they formed Velan in 2016, and I’ve always been struck by their ability to balance the business and artistic sides of making video games.
“Most of the work we’ve done is in the PC and console area, where the craftsmanship involved matters a lot,” Guha told me. “It’s not like we can crank out a prototype, put it out in a test market, look for KPIs, and optimize a perfect game. That’s just not how this part of the industry works. These are real artistic expressions.”
Over ten years, Velan has released six games and grown to 120 staff. But it’s not been a smooth journey. It’s faced project cancellations, job cuts, and then there’s the story of Knockout City. The ambitious live service dodgeball game was published by EA and attracted 12 million players, but it struggled to attract and retain enough players, and the game’s public servers closed down in 2023.
“Ultimately, we had to face some of the harsh business realities,” Karthik says “We showed it behind closed doors at E3 in 2018. We thought we had something. It was early days for live service. Then the landscape shifted a lot. It’s still a great game. We want to bring it back, but we have to do it differently. Enough things have changed that may make it more sustainable.”
Guha added: “It was a time when a season-based PvP, game-as-a-service game, was the thing to do. Structurally, they tend to have a lot of costs. There’s a server component, but there’s also just the amount of content you need to keep pumping out. So, it’s not a great venue to experiment with things that are truly out there. Maybe it’s okay for tried-and-true mechanics, but even that’s very high risk.
“There’s that, and also the dynamics of the market are changing very rapidly. Enabling technologies, consumer attention, where entertainment is coming from, and the nature of discovery. Developing a game that’s structurally high cost over multiple years, when the world around you are changing, is not the right way to approach innovation.
“We talked to a lot of experts after we launched, and it turns out the experts are better historians than they are forecasters. You never know what’s actually going to happen.”
Velan has modified its approach. It makes games in far shorter timeframes, and mixes these riskier concepts with bigger, double-A-level projects in partnership with IP and companies like Nintendo.
As a result, it’s expanding. Velan has just opened a new office in Toronto. And in today’s The Game Business, we are going to explore how it gained the trust of Nintendo, the opportunities around IP, the ideal business approach for mid-sized studios, and overcoming the cost challenges of making games in North America.
You can check out the full extended interview above, or read the highlights below
Sponsored Message
Create a new revenue stream for your PC game
Your own store, alongside the storefronts you already sell on.
The PC studios still here in ten years will be the ones building direct relationships with their players now.
Selling direct means running your own PC game store alongside the storefronts you already sell on. You set the price, players buy from you, and you keep up to 95% of every sale. A launcher with your branding handles delivery and updates, and payments work in every market you sell in.
This is not meant to be a replacement for traditional storefronts. It is a new revenue stream alongside them, and more than 1,000 PC games already run one with Xsolla Publishing Suite.
See how it works for your PC game .
How to win over Nintendo
Velan has developed two first-party Nintendo games: 2020 mixed reality racing game Mario Kart Live: Home Circuit, and this year’s Switch 2 Star Fox remake.
It’s rare to see Nintendo trust independent Western developers with its treasured brands. It’s a very exclusive club. So how has Velan gained that trust?
“We’ve had a longstanding collaboration with Nintendo,” Guha explains. “Our first game with Nintendo was Spider-Man for Game Boy Color in 1998. From there, we’ve been on the launch of every system.
“People ask me, how you build relationships throughout the industry? “You make promises and you keep them, and you try to exceed expectations. If you do this consistently over time, you build trust, you build relationships, and you build interesting opportunities to collaborate. Over the course of 35-plus years, that’s what we’ve tried to do. Star Fox is just the latest output of that.”
Karthik added: “The Nintendo partnership is a very special and unique one, and the bar is really high in terms of what we need to make. But that’s always been the case. Even when we were third-party with Nintendo. And it helped us back then. We made really good games that Nintendo liked, which gave us the opening to have conversations.”
The Balas first worked with Nintendo IP at Vicarious Visions, via a collaboration with 2015’s Skylanders Superchargers.
“That was a big moment for us, because we finally were able to integrate Nintendo characters into one of our games,” Karthik says.
The middle path
Horror party game Midnight Murder Club (published by Sony) is one of Velan’s more experimental concepts
Velan’s strategy is to find a “middle path” for a game studio that is neither indie nor triple-A.
“We’re finding a natural cadence, where we can do a double-A-scope game with an established or licensed IP,” Karthik says. “That could be a partner project or a licensed IP that we’re directly licensed, and we can make a double A investment around that because there’s an audience. Then, with more original IP, or something really out there in terms of gameplay, we can make more of a triple-I level investment with an even smaller team.
“For a veteran studio that is not a garage band indie, and we’re not a multi-hundred-person triple-A [company], this feels like a natural sweet spot for us. It’s something that the industry has lost a little bit, and maybe it’s coming back. It seems like a more sustainable path.”
But isn’t the middle a dangerous place to be?
“Business school says don’t be in the middle of anything, as it’s a giant hole,” Guha acknowledges. “You should be at one extreme or another, because that’s where you get differentiation. There’s a classic collapse of the middle.
“But what we mean here by ‘the middle’, is that there are lots of opportunities with audiences that are not massive. So, the puzzle is: how can you make a remarkable experience for a fanbase that’s big, but may not be a size to support hundreds of millions of dollars in production?
“There are a surprisingly large number of opportunities in this space, but it requires a different mindset. Some companies solve it by having low-cost locations. Other companies solve it with technology and tools. Some companies solve it with genre specialization, where particular teams are highly productive in certain types of games. There are different solutions.”
The Balas observe that as large companies focus on the big franchises, that leaves a lot of audiences and IPs that aren’t being served.
“The deals and partnerships are out there, where it’s much more reasonable now because they want quality that gives longevity to the IP and brings in new audiences,” Karthik says. “There is actually more opportunity now than before.
“When you’ve got an audience undeserved in these niches, and you can really deliver for them, it’s a great forcing function of scope.”
This gets to one of the key reasons Velan Studios has endured during such a tricky time. It has a staggered slate, featuring bigger, IP-based projects with more stability, next to smaller, experimental concepts.
“ More independent studios should try to do that,” Guha says. “They tend to be single-product companies, and if the slate at the publisher changes, then that becomes a real challenge. Or if they’re solely investment driven and the metrics don’t show up in the product, then the funding gets cut off.”
Managing the costs of North American game development
Velan is based in Troy in New York State. And like most US game companies, it has to deal with the high costs of making games in the country.
“ We are finding this balance where we have these core teams that have been together a long time and operate really well together,” Karthik begins. “With that core team, we can figure out all the risky bits and what’s core to the game, and then we can partner with co-developers, outsourcing teams, or individual freelancers, for scaling up production.
“We were observing this trend when you get into the back-half of productions, where the costs really go up, and the risk also goes up, and it’s a nail-biter to the finish line. And you’re hoping you can get done on time and hit the quality bar. Or you’re at alpha and it’s, ‘is it fun yet?’ ‘Oh no. it isn’t. we need to iterate and tune’.”
The Balas felt that should be inverted where the risk is higher when the costs are low, and the ideal is to have a small, agile team figuring things out first, before scaling up using outsource options. But although outsourcing can help with costs, it isn’t a one-size-fits-all strategy.
“It is our philosophy to pay as much as we can for the best talent,” Guha says. “And we’ve also got a strong dollar. So, what are the tools and production methodologies available to us? Sometimes outsourcing can play a role. But each type of outsourcing is also a little different. Sometimes wholesale for certain types of work can be efficient, sometimes it’s highly inefficient.”
“If you don’t know what you’re trying to build, it’s going to cost you three times as much to do it outside than inside.”
Karthik adds: “North America is the most expensive place to do game development in the world. So, there’s a lot of talk about, ‘Okay, what’s the burn rate? What’s the cost per man-month? Where can we go cheaper?” But that doesn’t necessarily mean you get the same productivity. If an outsource team is half as expensive as your internal team, but it takes twice as long, or more than twice as long because you’re not set up effectively, or the relationship isn’t going well, it may end up costing more.
“But over time, you build these trusted partnerships. Ultimately, we’re all after factor productivity, not the burn rate. Not the cost per person-month.”
Guha again: “If you don’t know what you’re trying to build, or you don’t have those pipelines down, and you’re trying to still figure that out, it’s going to cost you three times as much to do it outside than inside.”
The next ten years
Knockout City may soon be returning
Ultimately, the Balas sounded hopeful for what comes next.
“The number of doomsayers... every two years, it seems like everything is done,” Guha said. “The dominant players are set, there are no new opportunities out there… it’s a harsh environment. And then somebody goes and surprises everybody. This keeps us hopeful.”
Meanwhile, for Karthik, success isn’t all about business growth.
“It’s not about the destination,” he concludes. “We made our first game Synnergist in college, and it was not successful. We thought we were going to be rich and famous, and neither one of those things happened. We were just left in a lot of debt. It was real downbeat. It was a moment of introspection in terms of what we enjoyed about it.
“And we realized, it was actually the people that we were working with day-to-day, that made it special and really fun. That’s why we do what we do. And we get to also bring joy to potentially millions of people.
“If we can keep doing that, that’s just awesome.”
Join us back on Thursday for big interviews all about Call of Duty and Star Wars. See you then.

text:

title: Sensor Tower 2026年9月全球手游收入与下载量排行榜 TOP10
author: Sensor Tower
text:
根据 Sensor Tower 应用表现洞察数据，《 王者荣耀 》在9月延续强劲的收入势头，这主要得益于中国核心市场的支撑。“月照长安”赛季上线，新英雄王维登场，游戏同时加入赛季限定召唤师技能“雾行千山”，并推出“旅行日记”主题战令皮肤。此次更新期间，游戏下载量和玩家支出均小幅上升，体现出新玩法与赛季主题外观有助于重新激发玩家兴趣并推动商业化。
《 ROBLOX 》9月表现强劲，期间多款新游戏内容与线上活动接连上线。《Showdown》主打节奏紧凑的动漫风格战斗，《GOAT Football League》则为竞技足球玩法增添了轻松诙谐的元素。本月的重点活动“The Hunt: Roblox 20” 围绕平台20周年展开，玩家可以在多个经典《ROBLOX》游戏中完成任务，赢取专属奖励。《Brookhaven RP》与《侏罗纪世界》展开联动，加入恐龙和全新载具；《Dungeon Heroes》则上线“龙之庆典（Dragon Festival）”战令，带来全新宠物、技能和外观内容。这些更新为玩家回流和付费提供了新的动力；同期，《ROBLOX》的收入势头也进一步增强。
其他头部收入游戏在9月通过持续推出主题活动维持玩家活跃度。《 Candy Crush Saga 》推出“音乐季（Music Season）”，玩家可以制作专属音乐作品并收集奖励；同时，游戏还与两位国际知名音乐人 Shania Twain 和 Zedd 合作，为活动增添明星效应，并提供赢取奖品的机会。《Pokémon GO》月初上线“GO Fest 2026: Mega Finale”活动，重点围绕超级超梦X和超级超梦Y的团体战展开。随后，《宝可梦地平线：系列》联动活动登场，推出特殊装扮宝可梦和主题奖励。月末上线的“丰收节（Harvest Festival）”则推出闪光啃果虫，为玩家带来新的收集目标，并将活动热度延续至10月。

2026年9月，全球玩家在 App Store 和 Google Play 上的移动游戏支出达到61.3亿美元，环比下降7%。在市场份额方面，美国以28.7%的总收入占比位居首位；中国（仅统计 iOS 端）以15.7%紧随其后；日本以12.4%位列第3。
在全球手游收入增长榜中，《 ROBLOX 》9月同样位居榜首。按 iOS 收入计算，美国、英国和加拿大是其排名前三的市场，其中美国的月度收入增量最大。与此同时，《 Dragon Ball Z Dokkan Battle 》在“Global Dokkan Campaign 2026”活动期间再度带动玩家付费。玩家可以使用游戏内货币抽取当期精选角色，包括弗利萨和超级赛亚人孙悟空，随后还有超级赛亚人孙悟饭和完美沙鲁登场。每位角色上线时，游戏收入均出现峰值。8月26日上线的《 Zeus: The God of Arrogance 》将强劲的首发势头延续至9月。随着初期下载热度回落，游戏收入仍保持稳健。9月16日，游戏还开放了新的服务器组，为玩家提供重新起步的机会和更充足的成长空间。

腾讯旗下的《 王者万象棋（Honor of Kings Chess） 》位列全球手游收入增长榜第7名，表现主要由中国市场带动。这款自走棋游戏支持6名玩家选用熟悉的《王者荣耀》英雄组建阵容，并通过多轮自动战斗展开对决。拍卖机制、特殊技能和效果牌为每场对局增添变数，甚至可能改变战局。熟悉的英雄降低了《王者荣耀》玩家的上手门槛，而多样的阵容组合也为对局带来了不同的策略选择。

2026年9月全球手游下载排行榜 TOP 10

《 ROBLOX 》9月再次位居全球手游下载榜榜首。平台丰富的创作者打造内容为玩家提供了多种类型的游戏体验，社交功能则让好友能够相互发现并一同游玩。多元内容、好友共玩体验与源源不断的新内容，帮助《ROBLOX》保持广泛吸引力并吸引新用户。
《 Free Fire 》9月继续稳居全球手游下载榜第2名。9月16日，游戏再度推出与人气忍者题材动画《火影忍者疾风传（NARUTO SHIPPUDEN）》的联动活动。玩家可以探索动画中的木叶村，并完成任务，免费获得雏田或自来也主题的时装。熟悉的场景和可收集奖励，为动画粉丝带来了重返游戏的新理由。
《 Bus Fever Party! 》9月在全球下载总榜排名升至第5名，并位居下载增长榜第1名。该巴士分类解谜游戏由 Lumi Games 发行，自2025年6月上线以来累计下载量已超过2,100万次，印度、巴西、美国、墨西哥和印度尼西亚是其主要市场。玩家通过移动巴士、将乘客与对应车辆匹配来疏导交通。简单的操作、色彩鲜明的画面和难度逐步提升的关卡相结合，既降低了上手门槛，也为游戏保留了一定的策略性，有助于其吸引不同市场的玩家。

《 Brain Puzzle 3: Crazy Mind 》9月跻身全球手游下载增长榜，并在全球下载总榜上上升16位，升至第7名。该游戏由 Smallstep Technology 发行，将幽默风格的卡通情景与谜题相结合，鼓励玩家寻找出人意料的解法。简单的点击和拖动操作，加上贴心提示，让游戏容易上手；多变的剧情转折则让玩法保持新鲜感。印度尼西亚、菲律宾、巴西、俄罗斯和墨西哥是其主要市场。
《 MiniMuse 》于9月上线后位列全球手游下载增长榜第8名，主要市场包括美国和巴西。玩家可以设计角色、搭配服装并创建场景，讲述自己的故事。这些功能让游戏体验不止于换装，还为玩家提供了探索时尚、展现创意的更多方式。与此同时，《 Keyboard Escape: +1 Speed ASMR 》、《 Color Block: Combo Blast 》和 Supercent 发行的《 Bulldozer Master 》分别位列下载增长榜第4、第6和第10名。三款游戏分别以障碍闯关、方块解谜和放置挖掘为核心玩法，在熟悉的玩法基础上提供了清晰的成长目标。
总体来看，9月下载榜展现了成熟热门产品的持久吸引力，也体现出新作的发展潜力。社交玩法与知名 IP 帮助头部产品保持热度，而易上手的解谜玩法、创意自定义内容和熟悉的游戏主题，则为新玩家提供了多样化的入门选择。这些表现表明，无论是内容丰富的游戏，还是玩法鲜明的产品，都能在全球市场吸引大量玩家。
